title: AQA English Language Paper 1 Question 3: Structure (2026 Format)
description: AQA Paper 1 Question 3 structure guide for the 2026 format: 8 marks, whole-text movement, focus, pace, perspective, pivotal moments and practice method.

children: Paper 1 Question 3 is worth 8 marks and assesses AO2 through structure. From the first assessment in 2026, AQA gives learners a specific effect to focus on and offers clearer prompts about structural choices. That makes the target more explicit: explain how the source is organised and how that organisation creates the named effect across the text.
What counts as structure?

Structure is about the arrangement and movement of the text, not simply the presence of a technique. Useful choices can include shifts in focus, changes in pace, contrast, a pivotal moment, changes in mood or tone, perspective, foreshadowing, flashback, withheld information, cyclical patterns and the relationship between the opening and ending.
Where does the writer direct our attention at the start?
What changes, and at what point?
What information is delayed, revealed or repeated?
Does pace accelerate or slow?
Does the mood, tone or perspective shift?
What is different about the ending, and why does that matter for the named effect?
Use movement, not a shopping list

The most useful structural sentence often contains a movement: “The focus shifts from… to…”, “The pace slows before…”, or “The ending returns to…”. Structure is easier to analyse when you describe change.
A whole-source method
Identify the named effect in the question. Keep it visible in every paragraph.
Map the source quickly as beginning → development → ending. Write a few words for what changes in each stage.
Choose two or three structural movements that genuinely shape the effect.
For each movement, explain why the writer positions it there and how the reader’s understanding or expectation changes.
Link separate moments together. Strong responses show how one section prepares for, contrasts with or transforms another.
Mini-example: analysing a shift

Imagine an extract that opens with a child waiting alone at a quiet station, then shifts to the approaching sound of a train, and ends with the platform empty again. Simply saying “the focus changes” is incomplete. A stronger analysis explains that the initial stillness establishes vulnerability; the shift to sound increases pace and expectation; the return to emptiness at the end can make the encounter feel unsettling or unresolved.
The 2026 change matters

AQA’s updated Question 3 now supplies a particular effect for candidates to consider. Do not ignore that wording and deliver a memorised paragraph about “zooming in” or “cyclical structure”. Treat the named effect as the thread joining your structural observations.
Common mistakes
Analysing individual words as though this were Question 2.
Retelling what happens in chronological order without explaining why the arrangement matters.
Listing “focus shift, foreshadowing, climax” with no developed effect.
Writing only about the opening and ignoring the development or ending.
Using memorised claims such as “the writer zooms in like a camera” where the text does not support them.
Practice routine
Take an unseen fiction extract and divide it into three or four structural stages.
Give each stage a five-word label.
Draw arrows showing the main changes in focus, pace, mood or perspective.
Choose one change and write why it occurs at that point.
Add a second paragraph explaining how a later structural choice develops or reverses the earlier effect.
Final checklist
I wrote about the source as a whole.
I described structural movement, not just events.
I linked choices to the specific effect in the question.
I explained positioning and development.
My terminology describes what the text actually does.
